title: The Secret Language of Cat Licking: Friendship, Peace Treaty, or Warning?
summary: You've probably seen it: one cat pinning another down and licking its head like a tiny, furry hairdresser. Most people assume it's affection. But scientists who study cat behavior say that licking — called allogrooming — is a lot more complicated. In a 1998 study, researchers watched 25 cats living together in an indoor-outdoor enclosure. They found aggressive behavior in about 35% of allogrooming sessions. That's a big clue that licking isn't just about friendship. The authors suggested it might help cats defuse tension in a confined space, where a real fight would be too risky. To dig deeper, Morgane Van Belle, a cat behavior scientist at Ghent University in Belgium, and her team analyzed videos from 53 two-cat homes. They found that allogrooming seems to have different social functions depending on the situation. When cats licked each other while huddling and copying each other's body postures, it probably strengthened their bond. Most licking was aimed at the ears — an area packed with sensory nerve endings, which may help cats relax. Allogrooming calms other animals too: it lowers heart rates in horses and triggers feel-good hormones in monkeys. But the same behavior can also mean something else. Sometimes licking led to friendly wrestling — grabbing with front paws and tumbling around — suggesting it's a signal to start play. In other moments, licking was followed by conflict signs like ears turning backward, pawing, and biting. One cat would stand over the other, and both showed subtle stress signals like lip licking or head shaking. The researchers think allogrooming may be an "appeasement signal" — a way to calm things down when a fight could break out, like when one cat wants another's sleeping spot. Similar behavior appears in meerkats, where lower-ranking ones groom dominant ones to keep the peace. Yet because licking often targets the neck — the same spot cats bite during fights — it might also be a subtle threat. Van Belle's team also suspects allogrooming helps with hygiene, since it targets the head and neck, the areas cats can't easily reach themselves. But the study didn't measure dirt or parasites, so that's still unproven. Dr. Terry Curtis, a veterinary behaviorist, thinks the explanations are reasonable but not final. After 25 years of studying cats, she's skeptical anyone will ever fully decode them. "Congratulations, you got a cat," she said. "Let the mystery begin."
why_it_matters: Learning to test what animal behavior actually means — instead of assuming it — is the same skill scientists use for every claim about the world, and the same skill you need when you try to read the intentions of classmates, siblings, or even pets at home.

background_read: Humans have lived with cats for thousands of years, yet cats stayed partly wild: unlike dogs, they were never bred to obey people, so much of their body language still comes from solitary hunters that avoid fights whenever they can. Scientists who study animal behavior therefore treat a lick as data, not as a hug.

One useful comparison is the meerkat (a small mammal from southern Africa that lives in tight groups), where lower-ranking animals groom dominant ones to keep the peace — the same 'appeasement' logic the cat researchers describe. Monkeys and chimpanzees do a version of it too: they groom allies to build friendships and calm rivals, and grooming releases feel-good brain chemicals such as oxytocin.

Ghent University in Belgium (a research university known for animal-behavior work) is where Morgane Van Belle, a cat behavior scientist, led the video study of 53 two-cat homes. The article also quotes Terry Curtis, a veterinary behaviorist (an animal doctor who specializes in why animals behave the way they do). Because cats cannot tell us what they mean, researchers rely on careful video coding — who started, where the lick landed, and what happened next.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a richer view of cats
perspectives.description: The research shows cats have a complex social toolkit, not just an on-off switch for affection. Owners of multi-cat homes can read the signals — backward ears, lip licking, one cat standing over another — and reduce stress before a real fight happens.

The samples are small and based mostly on watching videos, and the hygiene idea was never tested because no one measured dirt or parasites. Critics warn that owners may over-read the results, either as proof that their cats love each other or as proof of bullying.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — it fits a wider pattern
perspectives.description: Allogrooming is common across mammals: meerkats use it to keep peace, monkeys use it to build alliances, horses relax when groomed. The cat data is less a unique cat mystery than one more example of animals using touch to manage group life.

Larger, longer studies that combine video with hormone tests and heart-rate sensors could show whether a given lick is bonding, appeasement, or a quiet threat. Until then, the honest answer is that the same behavior probably means several things at once.
